content: 1. Infants were treated with one of three regimens: a single drug regimen consisting of six weeks of zidovudine (AZT), a two-drug regimen of six weeks of AZT combined with three doses of nevirapine (NVP) during the first week of life, or a three-drug regimen of six weeks of AZT plus an initial two weeks of nelfinavir and lamivudine (3TC). 2. The rate of intrapartum HIV transmission was significantly lower in the two-drug and three-drug regimens compared to the single-drug AZT regimen. 3. Serious adverse events, likely related to the study drugs, occurred in 4% of infants. The majority of these events were grade 2 or higher neutropenia and anemia. 4. Only two serious skin-related adverse events were reported, one in each of the two-drug and three-drug groups, but neither was attributed to the study drugs. Mortality rates did not differ between the study groups. 5. The HPTN 046 trial, conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, evaluated the efficacy of six months of NVP versus placebo in breastfeeding populations. Infants receiving six months of NVP had a 54% lower transmission rate at six months compared to those receiving only six weeks of NVP. 6. Most mothers in the study were not on antiretroviral therapy (ART) during pregnancy or postpartum. Among infants born to mothers receiving ART at the time of randomization, postnatal transmission rates were extremely low and did not differ between those receiving extended NVP prophylaxis and those receiving placebo. 7. Serious adverse events occurred in 16% of infants receiving extended NVP and 15% of those receiving placebo, with no significant differences in overall adverse events or mortality between the groups. 8. An observational study of 5,285 high-risk mother-infant pairs from eight European cohorts found that 88% of infants received neonatal prophylaxis, with 24% receiving combination prophylaxis. 9. Combination prophylaxis was associated with a higher risk of transmission, likely due to confounding factors such as maternal viral load exceeding 1,000 copies/mL at delivery. 10. Toxicity data from a subset of the cohort showed no significant differences in serious adverse events between infants receiving one, two, or three drugs. A trend toward more neutropenia events in the three-drug arm was observed but was not statistically significant. 11. A single-arm study in Thailand evaluated a regimen of AZT + 3TC + NVP for two weeks, followed by AZT + 3TC for an additional two weeks, in infants whose mothers received less than eight weeks of antepartum ART. This regimen reduced transmission rates compared to historical data when only infant AZT was used. 12. None of the reviewed studies addressed infants identified as HIV-exposed postpartum or those exposed to incident maternal HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding. However, the findings of the systematic review may be applicable to these scenarios. 13. Recommendations for extended prophylaxis in breastfeeding infants are based on maternal ART being initiated at or before the start of infant prophylaxis, as infant prophylaxis is intended to provide protection while maternal viral load decreases on ART. 14. High-risk infants are defined by factors such as incident maternal HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding, maternal viral load exceeding 1,000 copies/mL near delivery, or maternal ART duration of less than four weeks. 15. For high-risk newborns, an HIV polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test should be performed at the time of initiating prophylaxis to minimize the risk of resistance development and ensure timely ART initiation for infected infants. 16. Mothers living with HIV should exclusively breastfeed their infants for the first six months of life, introduce complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for the first 12 months, provided they are on ART. Breastfeeding should only stop once a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. 17. In settings where diarrhea, pneumonia, and malnutrition are significant causes of child mortality, breastfeeding combined with maternal ART and infant ARV prophylaxis is recommended to reduce HIV transmission risk while promoting infant survival. 18. In other settings, complete avoidance of breastfeeding may be recommended. 19. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of breastfeeding in the first 12 months of life to prevent mortality from diarrhea, pneumonia, and malnutrition, with a low risk of HIV transmission when the mother is on ART. 20. Research gaps include the need for data on postnatal ART adherence, patterns of retention in care, and the duration of breastfeeding among women living with HIV. 21. Further studies are needed to evaluate the shortand long-term health outcomes of infants exposed to prolonged, low-dose ARV drugs, including their effects on neurodevelopment, growth, renal health, and bone health. 22. Sentinel site monitoring of infant cohorts during the first two years of life is recommended to better understand the implications of ARV exposure through breastfeeding on resistance and toxicity. 23. Operational challenges in providing multiple drugs to newborns highlight the need for simplified dosing regimens and better formulations, such as dispersible fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets suitable for infant prophylaxis. 24. Provider training and innovative approaches to dosing, such as twice-daily NVP administration, are critical for successful implementation of these recommendations. 25. Research into alternative drugs for infant prophylaxis, such as integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), which may be better tolerated and more effective, should be considered. 26. National health authorities should decide whether to counsel and support HIV-infected mothers to breastfeed while receiving ARV interventions or to avoid breastfeeding entirely, depending on the local context. 27. WHO is considering whether to recommend unrestricted breastfeeding for mothers living with HIV who are on ART, as well as enhanced monitoring for potential toxicities from prolonged infant ARV exposure through breast milk. 28. The effects of ARV drugs on neurodevelopmental outcomes, growth, renal health, and bone health in infants need further investigation. 29. For infants who become HIV-infected despite prevention efforts, ARV exposure through breastfeeding has implications for resistance and toxicity, potentially affecting the success of ART regimens for the child.
